utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. Oh, sorry, yes, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe we tried to be fairly specific here. In fact, we've identified specific minutes by date, specific orders, and then again we've tried to ask them for documentation relating to the incidents set forth in the indictment. So we have again limited the scope of our inquiries to those areas that the Prosecution alleges the criminal responsibility of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in relation to 16 (D), that's again the most serious incident, you're saying a request has specified these already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That one asks for documents that -- from all the incidents in the indictment, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All the incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, this one does not relate to the 12 incidents that were previous -- related to the municipalities set forth in the indictment and the time periods in the alleged occurrences in the indictment, as alleged by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now (D) -- oh, sorry (E), you have received something under that call have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the response from the Ministry of Defence has been to say we are preparing certain documentation that we will send to you which we have not received and, by the way, we are going to be opening our archives to you. So I believe that's a much smaller category of documents, but again I don't believe we've actually physically received anything. We've just received just recently the invitation to go into the archives and we have started to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the 16, the very last one, (G), have you not actually got these from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have unofficial copies and we don't know whether they're complete. We're just asking for the government to confirm they're -- that what was adduced at trial are official documents and whether they are complete or whether there are any additional pages, annexes, that are missing. That's pretty much the gist of that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it looks as though there may be one more, according to the response to -- there's one been identified of six pages that's being processed at the moment. But you haven't received that, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe we've received that, Your Honour, no. But they have advised us that they are preparing documentation for us. So I don't know if it's in the process of being sent or if it's in the mail already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvetkovic, I'd be grateful if you followed the same order and dealt with these matters as specifically as you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour, but it is very difficult, and I would like first to apologise, of course, that we haven't submitted our further response. However, we couldn't actually do that because the Defence completely ignored our annex (A), which was filed with our response to their motion. And, as you could see, we needed this hearing for the Defence to go through their requests and say what has been produced and what haven't been produced. However, I will try, of course, to go again through all the requests. And I hope that you have received what is entitled "updated annex (A) to Serbia response." I gave it before the hearing to the court officer. There were four copies of that, so -- okay. There are just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we haven't got it yet, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I've got a copy of that either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I hope they could be distributed before; however, there are some additions there. Before I begin with specific points, I would like to say just one more general point. I do believe that the requests of the Defence are very broad and they overlap a lot. And a lot of points here overlap with other points. And if you, for example, take a look at the so-called dossier KiM, I mean, that dossier encompasses all the other documents as far as I can see or, for example, the point where they ask for documents previously produced to the Office of the Prosecutor. Again, that point encompasses a various range of other documents which are sought under other points. And therefore, it is very difficult to answer this motion specifically and to say: Okay, we have produced this and we haven't produced that. And I believe that specification of the Defence would really be required, and especially having in mind our response and annex (A) to our response a specification of what they still want, since we have produced -- as was acknowledged today and in their reply, we have produced some 45.000 pages of documents so far. Now, if we start with this point (A) that was paragraph 12, I believe, from the motion. Well, first, Your Honour, there is a problem here with the translation. The translation -- their request in Serbian and the request in English. In Serbian the request asks for archives -- and I will switch to Serbian: [No interpretation] [In English] I'm going back to English. While in English it asks for daily and monthly official reports. If you ask for the assistance of the translator they will tell you that "casopis" is a magazine in Serbia, in Serbian, and not "official report." Now, this request was sent originally to the National Council in Serbian and I especially made an inquiry -- as I am not here in Belgrade I am here in our embassy, but before coming here I made an inquiry by the phone and I ask about this Albanian-language thing, and I was told that the request, original request specifically say "magazines" in Albanian language. That is what I was told from the people -- from the National Council. Of course, if we may -- perhaps Mr. Ivetic can assist us if we can take a look at that request because I haven't been able to see it in Serbian and that original request. Because if you -- I mean, if you take that these are official reports, then these requests overlap a lot with other requests. For example, the request under (R), daily and regular evidence and activity reports of the OUP and SUP stations in Kosovo. It's almost the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, it overlaps with -- did you say (R)?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I said (R), yes. (R) for example, but with a lot of others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, if they are official reports and not magazines, as I said, because the Serbian word used here means magazines or newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but your response indicates that you understood the words because it refers to the -- the documents as reports, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, I've got an updated annex. You've just given me the document and it refers to them as daily and monthly official reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I honestly believe that the person who wrote this just used the same translation as the Defence because I did ask what was in the request. I asked that two days ago people by phone, people from the National Council of Belgrade. I mean, I haven't seen the request. I asked whether it relates to magazines or to report. They told me magazines in Albanian, and this is what I received from Belgrade. So, yes, the translation is like that, but that is why I think the -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've got here in annex (A) what's being asked for in Serbian. It's not as if whoever's dealing with it from your side is simply accepting an English version of the request; it's there in Serbian and English on your own document. And you have chosen to refer to it as daily and monthly official reports. So I find it difficult to accept what you're saying, that you don't understand what was requested as being a report. There's a separate issue, and that is whether somewhere there is a reference to Albanian language. But where do you get reference to Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, Your Honour, I made an inquiry about this in Belgrade, I asked the people from National Council, I asked them how was the original request in Serbian language written. The answer was that they asked for "casopis," magazines, and magazines in Albanian language and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But casopis is a word which appears on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you've translated that as "reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where does the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It might be a mistake from the person in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And where is the reference to Albanian language in this statement in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no reference in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you'll not be surprised that I'm not persuaded at the moment by what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Not surprised. I guess you're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you understand that -- let me explain in a little more detail why we're doing this today. There have been occasions in the past where particularly the Office of the Prosecutor has claimed to have had great difficulty in dealing with the government of the Republic of Serbia and has alleged that there's been a lack of cooperation and that some of the responses have been less than frank. Now, I am extremely anxious before this trial starts to be sure that that is not the situation, that in fact we are being assisted by the government of the Republic of Serbia, particularly in the interests of the accused in this case, and it -- and here we have an application made by one of the accused. I'm not prepared to sit here and bandy this sort of exchange around about the language that's being used because that certainly gives me the impression that there's an attempt being made to evade the obligation to cooperate. And it seems to me that in this particular instance there is no substance in what you're saying. However, that subject I think was a perfectly reasonable request on your part, and that is that Mr. Ivetic should produce the original request. Now, I wonder if he can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to look through the documentation myself, Your Honour, to find that particular request. And if I find it, I'll be able to read it in Serbian. But that was one of our earlier requests. As I indicated we have in addition to this stack much more documentation linked to requests that I would have to go through. I did find the 12 incidents so I could recite those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I think if there is to be greater specification provided, it will be done after this hearing is over. I just, at the moment, want to be sure that we've explored the issues as far as we can in a hearing before making a decision about how to progress further. And it would be helpful if you were able to locate that document and let us have a look at it, although at the -- in the absence of it then there may be little reason to doubt that it contains the words that are set out in the Republic of Serbia's own annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I can add some clarification. All the requests were written in Serbian by my Serbian staff in Belgrade. So the requests were done in the native language, as were all the meetings that were held. So the issue of translations I don't believe should be that much of an issue, but I will endeavour to find that request if you want to continue with any further. If I find it I'll bring it to Your Honour's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a suggestion to make, with Your Honour's permission. Now is it possible for both of you gentlemen - as I see from you, you both have a desire to resolve the issue - to kindly sit down together and between yourselves find what documents are required, what are not required, and then you prepare a list of what is really the residual part. After you have received whatever you have received and after whatever essential is the residual part, and he has an acquaintanceship with that so that when he goes back or refers it back to the concerned authorities for getting those documents, it should be -- it will be a smooth exercise. Otherwise, I think we'll be rather lost quite a bit. Everybody will be looking and asking what to do and what not to do. Can't you have a conference on this? I mean there's nothing. It's on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would be more than happy to have a conference with them. We've had 23 conferences with the government of Serbia and Montenegro about these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: This conference will be under our supervision, because conferences you may have had is a different thing. But it will be right in our supervision and we can inquire tomorrow and later on what have you done and decide this issue so that we proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As Your Honours know, I'm here through the end of next week, so I've got plenty of time to sit down and discuss with them if that's something they're inclined to do. We -- like I said, I could prepare a list and bring copies to them of the original Serbian-language requests and we could sit down with them and go through with them item by item, but I'm just afraid that at that point in time we are extending so many efforts away from other trial preparations that, of course, we have to undertaken given the pre-trial and the trial on Monday. But on this particular issue I would be more than happy to. I'm sure I can locate the request, if not tonight by sometime tomorrow and if the gentleman would like to sit down and look at the requests -- is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What is your view on what I have said? Would you not like to sit and have it resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- as I already said, I believe that the Defence should have made further specification after we filed our response with their reply. And for that reason, we perhaps would have avoided an hour of Mr. Ivetic going through every point led by His Honour Judge Bonomy in the beginning of this hearing. So I do believe that a further specification would be very useful. In a way, I don't think that I am in a position to do that here, from the embassy of Serbia here, because it's -- the National Council is in Belgrade who deals with the requests and who -- and which has access to the material. Then I'm willing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interfering. Would you be kind in getting the right person immediately so that he answers the query, because otherwise to a remote working of these documents may we not -- and we may have to take some measures then. The question would simply be, why can't you can kind enough in asking somebody, the person responsible, to come over here and sit with the learned counsel from this side and both should resolve this. This has been happening or it happened in other areas where other jurisprudence were. And we have the alternate dispute resolution and so on, and this can be done outside instead of our taking up every little thing. I mean, you know what is to be given, what has been given; there must be a receipt about that. There must be documentation of what is given and what is left out. We should be -- with permission of the chair we should be available to be even interrupted if there is a difficulty on this, even at our chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm ready to sit with Mr. Ivetic, if you want today or tomorrow and to go through this. I'm not sure that I'm the one person to resolve it. However, for someone to come from Belgrade here, I guess it's not possible to have it done tomorrow, but for the next week I will write today or tomorrow morning to Belgrade and tell them about your request and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvetkovic, it seems to come to this in relation to (A), that there's been no search made for documents in Serbia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph (A).

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at the very first item on your annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The updated version is exactly the same as the previous version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It comes to this, that no search has been made for documents in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: In Serbian language, you mean. Yes, well, I mean, this is the answer which I have received from the National Council. As I -- I would like to say one thing, Your Honour, because you made reference to the 54 bis proceedings in the Milosevic case and I have to say that I'm glad that you have been involved in those proceedings because you have the experience from which we can benefit. And I'm sure that you are aware of the way in which the Office of the Prosecution filed their requests. In those proceedings they were very precise, usually, although the requests themselves might have not been that precise, but at least they were precise in what they asked this Trial Chamber to order. And they usually had annexes with their requests, and those annexes were those specific requests for assistance from which the Trial Chamber could see what was actually requested and of course we could see and -- what to reply to. All this is missing here. And we are speculating -- now we are speculating on what is written in the original submission of the Defence when there is an obvious mistake in translation of the word "casopis," "magazine," from Serbian to English. And of course we have our response which, in my opinion, is also a mistake which I have received from Belgrade and I haven't drafted it. I do apologise. I believe that we are missing key elements to decide here and I believe that those key elements which we are missing is a further specification from the Defence what is that they want. And then we can reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, show me where in your response you take the line that there is not sufficient specification for you to deal with these. I know that you say they're far too -- they cover far too much ground or too cumbersome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is it. For example, paragraph 8, the Defence of the accused Lukic did not identify the particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 it says from what I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is in your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is our response, yes. For example, it relates to the documents previously produced to the Office of the Prosecutor. And here we said: The Defence of the accused Lukic did not identify the particular documents which were not produced to the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that request is for everything that you've given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that is a problem because, as you know, in Kosovo and Metohija, I mean the OTP has been requesting documents since 2001 and there have been various bodies dealing with the cooperation with the ICTY and with the OTP. And we have produced a number of documents to the OTP from 2001 until now relating to Kosovo and Metohija. It's very difficult now to go through all those documents. It's almost impossible because our people have changed. For example, in the beginning it was the Ministry of Justice of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which does not exist anymore, which dealt with those requests. It's almost not possible to answer this request in whole. On the other hand, it is covered more or less by the other answers. I mean, the dossier KiM which they ask, dossier Kosovo and Metohija, it covers everything from what I could see. It covers all documents ever issued which is in connection with Kosovo and Metohija from what I can see here. And if that is not on over-broad request, I don't know what is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: From the outset I indicated to you that the essence of this dispute is availability and accessibility and that is what you're confirming just now, that there are certain difficulties associated with locating material here and making it available. But it's, to be sure, just to what extent these difficulties are going to inhibit the process of recovering the documents that we've been having this hearing. And I want to continue to deal with these items specifically. And it may be that we have to enter up a while before we continue with that. Mr. Sabbah, what is the position. We've been here for an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I believe that the interpreters would need some time for a little break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you just give us five minutes, then we'll have the break in a moment. If you take the second item, Mr. Cvetkovic, item (B) ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want my response? Well, first we heard from the Defence that documents were partially produced. And here I also have the information in this updated annex (A) that 130 pages of documents were forwarded to the National Council and they are awaiting decision from the government of Serbia. I know that there is -- today there is a session of the government of Serb. I don't know whether the government had adopted the adequate decision for -- to pass those documents. But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What could be the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any problem. The only problem might be that, for example, it's not on the agenda but on the other hand I don't see any reason why it wouldn't be on the agenda. It's just that I cannot guarantee that the government adopted this because I'm not there in the government. But I know it has been sent to the agenda of the government so it should be in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's specific enough. In, of all places, Belgrade, it should be appreciated just how urgent it is to get this material because it's been known for some time that this trial would start on Monday. And the material's been available since the 26th of May, and still not available to the Defence. Now, do you think that's a reasonable position to be in?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say it is a little longer than usual, even -- usually the time is, let's say, two to three weeks from the production of the documents to the National Council until the documents are passed to the Defence or to the OTP because that's the time required for the session of the National Council and of the government to take place, from what I remember when I was working there in Belgrade in the National Council. So I would say, yes, in this time it is a little longer than necessary, but usual time -- little longer than usual, but usual time is around three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have a break and we'll resume at quarter to. The -- you can take it that we accept that certain things have to be made much more specific than they are, and that's particularly in light of what Mr. Ivetic has already acknowledged and undertaken to improve upon. So that part you need not be too concerned about. But there are still elements in the responses that do need to be clarified before we can make an adequate order that does justice to both parties' requirements and difficulties. For example, I need to -- I for my own part need to hear more about the difficulties of the codes that have been used for some of the documents. And there may be other matters. So we will look at these and other relevant matters when we return at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cvetkovic, you've managed scare off Mr. Ivetic. That's one way of achieving your objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvetkovic, the next item is item (C), and the -- the submission made by Mr. Ivetic on that was that the material supplied was inaccessible. He's been given CDs that -- to which he cannot get access.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't seen the CD. From what I heard, it is true that some of the documents are a little difficult to open on the CD, but that's the minority of the documents, while the majority may be opened. However, I believe this is purely a technical matter and I really don't think that someone from the BIA would just give that CD to mock at the Defence, I mean give them the CD with documents which cannot be opened. So perhaps it's a technical matter, and I think it can be solved very easily in Belgrade. I don't think we can solve it here because the documents are back in Belgrade. But I don't think that an order from the Trial Chamber would be necessary for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, remind me the paragraph in your response that deals with this -- or your reply, rather. Can you remind me of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph in the reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- that deals with that. Yeah, that was Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's the BS -- CDs of which one couldn't be opened at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you actually set that out in the reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the first point -- are you able to deal with it, Mr. Cvetkovic, that there's missing software?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not aware of any particular software which opens -- some special software which opens documents. And if such software exists with B, I don't think they would just give it away like that. So it may be that some documents are not burned properly on the CD or that there is something wrong with some documents that it cannot be opened. But from the information I have it doesn't relate to all the documents -- actually, to the minority of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the second point that's made is the ones that he has been able to get access to are all in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we heard something differently today from what I heard from Mr. Ivetic because that -- or that's not what we heard, that those documents which can be opened are only in Albanian. We heard that there are documents which are Albanian -- in Albanian and that there are Serbian translations but that is too much of a trouble for them to match them and to make -- I don't know, to put them in some order. We could maybe -- we could maybe look that up or ask Mr. Ivetic to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who is the person he should make contact with to evolve this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he should make contact with the National Council, and actually I was informed that some people who worked for the Defence of the accused have already contacted the National Council. And I think that the matter is being looked at -- not at this very moment properly because it's after working hours there, from what I know these day. So I think that they already contacted the right people in Belgrade; I think we can just expect for it to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your response lists 25.000 documents as the first item -- in fact, I think that is the total, is it, 25.000 and then you break it down?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that's what it says there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these -- are you saying that these are on the CDs?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, according also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may just say, according to this new version of this annex (C), there are now 24 DVDs which are -- which have been delivered to the National Council and which are waiting for the decision of the National Council and the government to be passed to the Defence. They've been delivered on June 28th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: That's towards the end, close to the end of this annex A under (C), under documents sought from the Army of Serbia and Montenegro, since the documents sought are more or less the same. I mean, it says just relevant investigative documents on the organisation, operation, structure, command, financing, army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that. We'll come to that. That's when we deal with the army. What we're dealing with is the Ministry of the Interior at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, however there are documents which have been, for example, communicated both to the army and the Ministry of the Interior and there is certainly a large number of the documents which were shared between the two -- the two structures. So I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, for clarification, the BA is now a separate agency so it's not technically the Ministry of the Interior, it's the BIA that provided these CD-ROMs that, again, on of them could not be opened at all, and the ones that could be opened had instructions for running an operatable programme which was supposed to allow us to view and print the documents and when you try to click on it, it asks -- it says that the file is missing and cannot open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes -- just while you're on your feet can you clarify one other thing. There's reference in the response to a number of documents and there are a number of dates. So there must be more here than is said to be on the CDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would imagine there was -- I believe there was a reference to some DVDs that have been sent to the National Council that have not yet been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's separate. If you look at the updated response, you'll see that it refers to 25.000 pages relating to the KLA activities passed to the Defence team on the 31st of May. Now, have you got that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As of right now, whether that's on the CDs or not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because I just received this while we sat here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next refers to a date, the 20th of April, photocopies of statements. Did you get these? That's two different dates, you see, the 31st of May and 20th of April. Now, did you get all your CDs on the one date?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The CDs I believe were on the one date. I believe this other -- this other material, I believe, is material that we have received. But the CDs was what was the main concern of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's the 31st of May, the CDs, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that sounds accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you accept that you've got everything else here that's specified?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, having just received this during these proceedings and without having the entire file here, I can't 100 per cent verify it, but as I indicated we received some cooperation following the filing of our motion and had begun receiving material from them but there is a large volume of material that, it's my understanding, is waiting to be sent to us and has been in that state for at least over a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are these CDs at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe that they're at Belgrade at the office of our investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you have an investigator there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any reason why contact can't be made with the National Council with a view to having this resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's my understand that contact's already been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There's nothing prohibiting that, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been told it's a technical issue. Surely we are not expected to resolve technical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope that it is something that can be resolved. As indicated we have contacted them and informed them of the CDs. I know I personally reviewed the CDs and the defects in them when I was in Belgrade just two months ago, and I believe at that time we had already contacted BIA to complain of it and subsequently we have contacted the National Council. But indeed if that is all that they have relative to our request, that is something we would expect that they should be able to correct by just issuing new CDs. We're not talking about a huge number of CDs. We just believe that there might be other documentation in addition to that, given the types of responses that we've been hearing from them with respect to this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Cvetkovic, the next item is one, that's (E), is one in which Mr. Ivetic said he would be more specific. Number (F), however, was one where he mentioned a number of specific items that had not been supplied. Are you able to deal with these?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: With (F), Your Honour, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: (F), yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He mentioned that, for example, that Slivovo was one which had not been dealt with. He mentioned Racak and he mentioned material on KLA crimes, on the functioning of the police during the conflict, on NATO activities during the conflict, on the investigation of alleged war criminals. Are you able to say where there are documents that fall into these categories available but have not been provided yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there are documents which are still available and have not been provided with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, he again has said he'll be more specific on that, so we'll pass over it. On (G), which is this request for all that you've given to the OTP. The explanation -- I mean, it seems to me an inappropriate request at first reading this document. But the explanation given is that it's more manageable than trying to find the material among all the documents that are disclosed to the Defence by the OTP. Now, your answer, I think, earlier was that these documents will all be somewhere in other requests here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it goes back to the same problem, I suppose, of trying to get it from the OTP. It's -- if it was readily available in the form that it's sought here, then obviously that would be helpful. And the response you initially made indicated the possibility of that, that only one -- there had been one copy made but that was the copy given to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: It really depends, Your Honour -- I mean, unfortunately, as I said, there have been various bodies dealing with requests of the OTP since 2001. And, for example, when Ministry of Justice of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was dealing with those requests, from what I know they haven't made any copies of the documents that they then sent to the Office of the Prosecutor. They don't even have a very good register of what they sent. Okay. Then it was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs which was in charge. Now things were already better and I think that the archives of the requests definitely exist; however, I'm not sure whether all the documents which were produced to the Office of the Prosecutor exist in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. They sure exist in the Ministry of the Interior or the Ministry of Defence who passed them on to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Now for some two years or a little less, it is the National Council for cooperation which is solely competent of answering the requests of the Defence, while for the requests of the OTP the competence is divided between the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and the National Council. Basically, in order to answer this request of the Defence in total, you would have to go through all requests made by the OTP and see that all the documents that have ever been for the last five years produced to the OTP and all -- I'm not saying that we are not doing that back in Belgrade. All that I'm saying is that it is not possible, I think, to answer that request completely and just to say: Okay, this is all that has been produced to the OTP and we guarantee that there is nothing else that you may find on the EDS that has been produced by Serbia to the OTP. That is just very difficult to guarantee that. But we are definitely doing our best to comply with this request of the Defence and we have produced a large number of documents which have been produced to the OTP before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. If you move then to (H).

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have a follow-up on (H), unfortunately. There is this last sentence here saying that Ministry of the Interior informed National Council that it did find -- okay, there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a pity that it's taking so long once they are found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. Obviously they haven't been transferred to the National Council either, so I don't have a follow-up on that. I think -- I believe that they are still -- according to this at least, in the hands of the Ministry of the Interior, these remaining minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, number (I) is the first where we encounter this problem of encryption and response deals with this. Now, you initially referred to paragraph 15 which talks about the procedure for releasing documents which have been crypto-protected Telexes, but you have now moved on to a different position which is that on the 2nd of June the ministry told the National Council it doesn't possess Telexes from the minister of the interiors for the period May and/or June 1997. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's the latest information I have received from Belgrade on the status of this particular request. Of course, Your Honour, there is here again the question of translation because in Serbian it's singular, it's one document, while in English it's plural and it's like Telexes sent with an unspecified number, while in Serbian it is singular and it is one Telex, one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is this request designed to obtain one particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's our understanding that there is at least one document and we thought it was either May or June. It could have been two documents, one in May and one in June, but we are talking about either one or two documents in this particular section talking about the organisation and in particular the duties of a police general, which we believe should exist in the archives somewhere. We were about as precise as we could be with the date. We -- our client recalls it being issued and existing, but of course -- I don't know where to go with the initial response saying it is encoded and now saying that they don't have it. That leaves me at a loss for any kind of follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. It is one of these things that makes you concerned about this, Mr. Cvetkovic, that there's a response about encoding and then a statement that there isn't such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, from what I can see from paragraph 15 -- I mean, I've read -- read it, of course, before but I didn't expect this particular question to be raised here. This document, our response paragraph 15 does not say specifically that we have the document. And now suddenly we don't have it. Paragraph 15 deals in general with the requests for crypto-protected documents and there is not only one request of that kind. And I'm sure that crypto-protected documents may be found -- well, more or less under most of the points of the requests of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does that mean every Telex that is sent is crypto-protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There are specific -- I mean, there are cables. I'm sure you are aware of -- for different -- they are used in diplomatic practice, but they are also used, the ministries of internal affairs use those cables when they want to send some information which is strictly confidential. So they use it for their internal communication. The problem which we are facing here is that there is this special code which is used for encrypting those cables --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you're perhaps missing my point, that in paragraph (I) of your annex you say: See paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 15 deals with encryption of cables -- of Telexes. Why would you refer to paragraph 15 unless you were saying: Documents that fall under this head are crypto-protected?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because the word used in Serbian "depese" is a word used exclusively for cables, for crypto-protected cables. I've been working in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for four years. I know what is the word used for cables and this word "depese" is used for cables or -- at least to my knowledge that's the word we use for -- exclusively for crypto-protected cables. So I believe that that is what made people who wrote this response of Serbia and Montenegro refer to paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one point. When I met with members of the MUP and members of the Ministry of Defence, there was a clear distinction between depese and sifrovane depese, coded Telexes and regular Telexes. I don't know whether that helps any, but that was my understanding and my understanding is we are asking for a telex, which we at that time would not know whether it was coded or a regular Telexes. But there are Telexes that exist that are not encoded by this cryptographic system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Again, my understanding is different from you. When this particular word is used, it's crypto-protected communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, item (J) the complaint is that the documents delivered don't relate to the relevant period, which is 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, our argument is that they relate to relevant period and -- well, having here heard much from the Defence explaining why that it is they don't relate and we haven't heard much from him in answer to what was written in our annex (A). So I believe it's up to them to specify what is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, show me where you refer to documents for 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they are in the first one, the first paragraph, information about special operations unit, organisations, systemisation, which are describing the state security service internal organisation statute from April 1996 which were valid until November 22, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would be -- fall within the category of personal orders to commanders, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, again, it's not personal orders to commanders. Again, it's a wrong translation. It's personalno resenje, which are -- I cannot find an English word, but perhaps the translator --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Personnel solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: -- when you are -- when you receive a certain job, when you are given certain jobs. So that's an order what to do. It's order of appointment, if you want to -- I believe that's the correct translation. Again we have a problem with translation here. And of course we have -- we have documents which are used for appointment of those people. They say: Documents on criterions used to appoint those people in certain units and this is the document, the one which I quoted was the one which referred to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, under (K) --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I may just add. At the end of this long column you have state security service -- under the previous -- the previous point. State security service personal data relating to lists of personnel stationed in special units for period from 1992 to June 1999 as well as 12 separate resolutions and situating state security personnel. So basically that's it, that's what this request is about and not orders to members of these units what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you'll see at the beginning of the request it's talking about the operative acts on their formation and organisation and functioning. However, I agree with you that most verification is required of what's missing. I don't think you need to address this further. Item (K) --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well I don't have anything from what is written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the explanation is not very satisfactory, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are well-known bodies and you would expect reports on their activities to be easily located.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes and no because in a way if they are, for example, now under -- under -- if BIA is their successor. As far as I know BIA is successor of some of these units. So perhaps the documents are not in the Ministry of the Interior. Perhaps they are with BIA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure how easy it is to locate them, but anyway I agree that the response is not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In -- even though there's been a change in the organisation, this request, at least, is clear enough for even me sitting here in The Hague to understand very clearly what it's about. It's not one that depends on special -- particular special knowledge that's never emerged in general within the Tribunal. So you would expect that it would be possible to say what had happened to these records if they are not available or, alternatively, to have found them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. Yes, Your Honour. I would like to say that I still think that this request is also rather broad. For example, if those units were there every day, then you must have thousands of reports on their activities. And it is also -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can't have it both ways, Mr. Cvetkovic. You can't tell us that we haven't got anything at all or we're still looking and then tell us there must be thousands of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what is my opinion and it doesn't relate on the answer of the Ministry of the Interior. I'm trying to help you with my personal -- in this case it's my personal opinion, from my personal experience in working -- working for the National Council and for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and processing the requests of -- by the OTP and the Defence. For example, you have under -- under (F). Under (F), the documents which were provided by BIA, you have, for example, his discipline procedures, but then they have summary of important events from Kosovo and Metohija of July -- then from June 1st to June 10th on 3.713 pages. I'm sure that there you can find some reports on the activities of the special units here and there. So -- and it has already been produced to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think we're maybe speculating a bit on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the Defence has been speculating even more with their requests, which are too broad, in my opinion, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I, for one, don't agree with you that this one's too broad and it's disappointing to see that there is no clear explanation. Now, on the next one, (L), it's difficult for me to follow what exactly's being said in the latest document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, from what I can hear -- from what I can see here and the way I understand this is that these 85 cases which have been -- which have been produced to Defence, they relate to disciplinary proceedings against the personnel of the -- of the MUP, but not for these reasons that they are particularly requested that they refuse to serve in Kosovo but for some other offences, whatever they were. While they now informed, from what I can see on the 2nd of June, that they do not possess that particular information on disciplinary proceedings against MUP personnel who refuse to serve in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if that means there were no such proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- there is one more -- one more thing here, Your Honour, again. Because this is again a single document and this is, again, a single document in Serbian. When you read this, it's one single document and the Ministry of the Interior replied that they don't possess that single document. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say refers to a single document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, because in Serbian when you use a particular case, like this, "informaciju," [B/C/S spoken], that relates to a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, it's been translated as information and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, there is no "information" and "documents" in Serbian. It's just information on and documents is completely missing from Serb -- from the Serbian original in which - and we heard that also from Mr. Ivetic - all the requests were made. This is just one of the points of translation. I had a lot of them, as you could see during this hearing that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why would you pass 85 cases over if it's one document that you think is being sought?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, these 85 -- same 85 cases you can find under (E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that's not my question. Why would you hand over these 85 cases or mention them under this section if you consider that it's only one document that's being --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the person who wrote this also didn't understand at the time when they wrote this. We make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now -- so we have documents under (M) which are again the subject of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, for -- from what I can see here and from the information I have received, they have been forwarded yesterday to the National Council by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and they will be on the session of the National Council tomorrow and the only reasonable expectation is that the National Council will recommend that they be transferred to the Defence. And then we need the decision of the government of the Republic of Serbia to do that. Now, that's just the -- but of course they would be produced in a form which would not endanger the code, and that form means that certain part of the document which does not contain the text of the document but some information which are important for the code -- I don't know understand that either, that much, that -- because the people who work on that who understand that who are experts for crypto-protection. But however, that one part of the document has to be blackened while of course the substance of the document remains intact. And documents will be produced in that form, both to the OTP and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And (N) is another that's been -- well, do you know what the discussion -- does the National Council publish what it decides or is it private, confidential advice it gives to the government?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: National Council does not publish its decisions, no, no, it doesn't. Not available to the public, anyway, does -- it writes reports on its decisions and there's usually a press communique saying in general what has been decided by the National Council, but it's not published in the Official Gazette or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now (O) we can pass over. (P), reports on how NATO aggression disrupted communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing new. This is what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, that's another one that's surprising, isn't it? That it wouldn't be easy to either identify where it is or explain why it's not available?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I have no -- I have no explanation why they haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. And (Q), now what does the response in (Q) mean, the reports of the intrabureau are still in search procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it means the same as under (P) above. That means that they are still being searched for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it follow from that that there is a -- there was an intrabureau working-group investigating Racak?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess it does. I haven't seen the communication from the Ministry of the Interior, but I believe that what people who wrote this admission did and that they used the information that the Ministry of the Interior had used before then. So I believe they are being searched. That doesn't mean, of course, that they exist, but you could say that. I cannot say one way or the other because I don't know something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And (R), (R) is one in which Mr. Ivetic would be more specific. Can I take you now to 13 (D) -- oh, before we do that, sorry -- yeah, sorry, yes, 13 (D). It's said by Mr. Ivetic that there was this specification of 12 incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, should I answer to that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before -- I'm just trying to be clear in my own mind about this. No, I think -- sorry, I think I'm looking at the wrong one. Is that 6 -- do you jump from 12 to 16 in your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we do. Yes, there is one more mistake here because I can see here that point (D) is missed completely in the annex, so what is (D) here should be (E), and then it goes (E) (F) (G), and we missed (D). I just noticed that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we're now looking at -- is it 16 rather than 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: In our annex, yes, but if you want to go through 13, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at 13 (D).

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: 13 (D), yes, 12 most serious incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the problem there?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the problem there? Well, I don't see that there is a problem, but I believe that most of the documents have been produced and they have been produced -- I mean, first of all, as far as I know that when the original request was made those 12 most serious incidents were not specified. They might have been specified later, so somebody expected the minister of the interior to decide which are 12 most serious incidents from the indictment. However, I -- maybe they have been specified later. But if you go back and look at point (F), which deals with dossier of KiM. You can see there Izbica, Suva Reka, Krusa, Vucitirn, may all these places in Kosovo and the documentation have been produced. Perhaps not everything. Perhaps they're still missing something, but it's not like nothing here has been produced. That is what I said in the beginning, that these requests overlap a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And looking at 16 (E), which you've numbered as (D).

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's quite specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what you have discovered will be dealt with tomorrow. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, since I don't have an update in here, but if it's at the National Council, I believe it will be dealt tomorrow. I don't have an update here in this -- in this annex, but I believe it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In your life, what does the word "shortly" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "Will be forwarded to the Defence team shortly after the next session of the National Council."

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the next session of the National Council I think was held 19th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you said it normally meant two or three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in some instances we've seen here we are approaching two or three months without any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in this case if -- it was produced to the National Council on the May 26th. From what I know the first session of the National Council was on the June 19th and the first session of the government of Serbia since that is today. So if this document -- and I think it has -- it was on the National Council -- it should be on the government of Serbia today and which means it can be produced Monday, for example, to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the response says: The document is being processed and will be forwarded to the Defence team shortly after the next session, not of the government but of the National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As if it's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the document says, which I believe is not entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I presume -- so paragraph (D) is actually (E), and then if we go to (F).

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the material previously sought from the -- we've been over that already, yeah. And it will -- lastly numbered -- what is (F) must be (G). Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Or is it? No, I don't think it is, Mr. Cvetkovic, let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: 16 documents of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 16 is -- 16 (B) -- paragraph 16 does have a (D), so there's no need to change these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it has (D), which we have missed. It does have (D), yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you have actually dealt with it. So they are correctly numbered here. But you haven't dealt with (G). That's the joint -- oh, but you have, actually, so you'll called it (F). We're quite confused now. If this is paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the way I read it, it looks as if they have not responded to my 16 (D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They've missed (D), sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: (E) (F) -- so when they talk about (F) here, they really mean (G). Is that right? Is that right, Mr. Cvetkovic, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, when -- what is written here (F), that's (G), yes, 16 (G).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this document, it says is being processed at the present and will be forwarded at the next session of the National Council. That's similar to a request a moment ago, which you said wasn't up-to-date. What about this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, that's another of the document. I mean, first of all, I would like to go back to the 16 documents because we have the request for 16 documents plus two documents which are, by the way, included in those 16 documents which Mr. Delic brought to Milosevic case. So it's these 16 documents which, according to this information, have been passed to the Defence team on 10th of February, 2006, and still we have a request for binding order for those 16 documents. Now it seems there has been found this -- another document of the Joint Command from 1998 and I sincerely hope that this document will be passed up to today's session of the government of Serbia, but I don't have anything more on that. I would, however, if you allow me, like to add one general observation with -- well, with respect to all of the requests of the Defence, since we don't know when exactly have these requests been made and for how long have they been searching for -- for particular documents. Because what they say in their submissions that they are asking for those documents since November 2005; however, if you take a look at their list which is paragraph 23 of the motion, you can see a number of communications, and from what I -- from what I've been informed the communications are still arriving in the National Council. They are requesting documents all the time. So we don't know for how long have certain search being going on. So when you ask me: How can I explain that certain documents have not been found, it doesn't mean that they have not been found from November. Some of them have been requested in April or May. The Defence didn't make it clear in their submission when is that they first asked for a specific document. That's another -- well, I think what we miss in their submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Two things are plain from this hearing, and we will reflect on them in a brief written decision. One is that the requests need to be updated and need to take account of what's actually been received and be more specific in many instances about what is still sought. And the second thing that's clear is that some - I don't by any means say all - but some of the answers to these requests appear on the surface to be unsatisfactory and Mr. Cvetkovic was unable to amplify these explanations in a way which left us entirely satisfied with them. It's for us, I think, in that order to identify these particular areas. We're likely to follow a course which was followed earlier in this case in relation to another 54 bis application which is to give the applicant some time to present a fresh -- or at least to amend the application in a way that focuses it better. Now, Mr. Ivetic, it seems to me that you were -- or you felt earlier in the day that you would be in position to do this very quickly. Is that still the case or are you missing some of the material necessary to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Although some of the material is in Belgrade, I am in contact with our staff in Belgrade. And so I think -- with respect to outlining the specificity of what has been sought and what has been received, I can do most of that here with my staff here just by going through the requests that we actually sent to the government organs that have much of the specificity asked for and the dates they were requested, et cetera. And then in terms of determining what exactly was received, I should, I think, be able to communicate with my staff and be able to get something by the end of the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not so concerned now to have a complete procedural history of all that's happened, and I don't think Mr. Cvetkovic was making the point for that purpose. He was simply explaining that it's not clear in some instances how long the requests had been outstanding. But now we've got to this stage. How long they've been outstanding isn't terribly material. It's material to some extent when searches are going on, but beyond that it's not terribly material. So I'm more concerned that you tailor your requests to recognise what's been produced and to be more specific about what you seek and to try to be more economic about what you seek because there is so much repetition -- not repetition, but duplication and overlap here. We really need to cut that down. And I am concerned, just as an example, about the request about all the material that was given to the OTP. The explanation that it's been given to it's coming from so many sources does sound authentic and does sound like -- makes it sound like a request it would be very difficult to satisfy, whereas there are other ways of getting the material and you've enumerated a number of them already in separate requests. So if it's possible to combine it all into one more, as I said earlier, refined request, then that would be helpful. And I would like to think you could -- are you saying it will be available tomorrow or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can try and do that. I don't know how long the pre-trial is intended to last. I notice we're scheduled through the day from 9.00 to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It could be lengthy depending on the issues that we try to address. So if you're relying on tomorrow I can't expect you to have it done necessarily by tomorrow. But we're talking about a fairly brief period of time, and that will be reflected in the written order that we issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will do what we can do to issue that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, thank you for your assistance. The hearing is now adjourned.
